04 · Calculations
Calculating percentages, mg/mL and a child's dose
Type the answer as a number (a decimal fraction with a comma or a point). The solution is shown step by step after each problem.
Formulas
Mass from percentage:
substance (g) = total mass or volume × percentage / 100
mg/mL from percentage:
multiply the percentage by 10: 1% = 10 mg/mL, 2.5% = 25 mg/mL, 0.1% = 1 mg/mL
Percentage from ratio:
1:1000 = 0.1%, 1:5000 = 0.02% (percentage = 100 / the second number of the ratio)
Volume:
required volume (mL) = required dose (mg) / concentration (mg/mL)
Child's dose:
dose = mg/kg × body weight (kg)
Steady state:
Css is reached at about 4–5 × t½

About the model

The simulator is based on a one-compartment pharmacokinetic model: average literature parameters for adults are used. For phenytoin, saturable (Michaelis–Menten) elimination is used. In a real patient the values vary widely, so this is a teaching tool: in treatment the dose is chosen from the instructions, clinical guidelines and measured blood concentrations.

Stamp
The stamp and code of the medical institution. It shows in which institution the prescription was written.
Date
The day, month and year the prescription was written. The prescription's validity period is counted from this date.
Patient
The patient's surname, first name, patronymic and age. For children the age must always be shown: it is needed to check the dose.
Physician
The surname, first name and patronymic of the physician who wrote the prescription.
Invocation
The physician's address to the pharmacist: Rp.: (Recipe — take). Every drug begins with a new Rp.
Drug and quantity
The dosage form, the name of the drug substance (in the genitive case) and the quantity. The quantity is written in grams as a decimal fraction (0.5) or in milliliters.
Instruction to the pharmacist
Instruction to the pharmacist about the dosage form and the quantity to dispense: M.f. (mix, to make), D.t.d. N. (give … such doses), D.S. (give, label).
Method of use
How the patient should use the drug: the single amount, how many times a day, when in relation to meals, the route and duration. Vague words such as “internally” or “as known” are not written.
Signature and seal
The physician's signature and personal seal. Without them the prescription is not valid.
Paracetamol, tablet
Patient A., 30 years old
Acute respiratory viral infection. Temperature 38.8 °C, headache. No liver disease, does not drink alcohol.
Prescribe paracetamol as an antipyretic and analgesic in 0.5 g tablets (20 pieces). Write it in the abbreviated form.
Correct: after Rp. (take), a tablet is written in the accusative plural.
This is the nominative (plural). After Rp. the accusative is needed: Tabulettas.
This is the ablative (in tabulettis, used in the expanded-form instruction). In the abbreviated form, Tabulettas is written.
Name of the substance
Correct: the substance name is in the genitive (Paracetamolum → Paracetamoli).
Nominative. The name of the drug substance is written in the genitive in a prescription: Paracetamoli.
Ablative: only after “cum”, for example in a suppository (Suppositorium cum Paracetamolo).
Correct: 0.5 g = 500 mg.
In a prescription the dose is written in grams as a decimal fraction; writing “500” is an error: it should be 0.5.
5.0 g = 5000 mg: 10 times more in one tablet. This is close to a dose that causes fatal liver injury.
0.05 g = 50 mg: 10 times less, no effect.
Instruction
Correct: in the abbreviated form the number is shown on the Rp. line (N. 20), so only D.S. (give, label) is written.
D.t.d. is written in the expanded form. Here the number of tablets is already shown on the Rp. line and is not written twice.
M. (Misce — mix) is written only for dosage forms that are mixed up in the pharmacy. A ready-made tablet is not mixed.
Take 1 tablet when the temperature rises above 38.5 °C; at least 4–6 hours between doses; no more than 8 tablets (4.0 g) per day.
Correct: the single amount, the indication, the interval and the maximum daily dose are clearly written.
Take 2 tablets every 2 hours.
That is up to 12 g per day: the maximum daily dose for adults is 4 g. Such a dose leads to liver necrosis.
Take when the temperature rises.
The single amount, the interval between doses and the maximum daily dose are not given: the patient may choose the dose and overdose.
Internally.
“Internally” is a vague signature. How much, how many times a day and for how long must be stated precisely.

At high doses paracetamol forms a toxic metabolite (NAPQI) in the liver. In adults the single dose is 0.5–1.0 g, the maximum daily dose 4.0 g. In liver disease and alcoholism the daily dose is reduced.
Omeprazole, capsule (expanded form)
Patient B., 45 years old
Duodenal ulcer, Helicobacter pylori test positive. An eradication regimen (omeprazole + amoxicillin + clarithromycin) is being prescribed for 14 days.
Write the omeprazole of the regimen: 20 mg twice a day, 14 days. In the expanded form: the dose on the Rp. line, the number of capsules in D.t.d.
Correct: genitive (Omeprazolum → Omeprazoli).
Nominative. After Rp. the substance name is written in the genitive.
Ablative: used after “cum”, not needed here.
Correct: 0.02 g = 20 mg.
0.2 g = 200 mg: 10 times more.
The word “mg” is not written in a prescription: the dose is in grams as a decimal fraction (0.02).
2.0 g = 2000 mg: 100 times more.
Correct: 2 capsules a day × 14 days = 28 capsules, dispense in capsules.
14 capsules last only 7 days: twice a day × 14 days = 28 pieces are needed.
The dosage form is a capsule, so “in capsulis” is written, not “in tabulettis”.
In the expanded form the number of doses to dispense is shown with D.t.d. N.; D.S. alone is not enough.
Take 1 capsule twice a day, in the morning and evening, 30 minutes before meals, for 14 days.
Correct: proton pump inhibitors block active (meal-activated) pumps, so they are taken 30–60 minutes before meals.
Take 1 capsule twice a day after meals for 14 days.
Proton pump inhibitors are taken 30–60 minutes before meals: then they effectively block the pumps activated by food.
Take 1 capsule once a day for 3 days.
In an eradication regimen omeprazole is given twice a day for 10–14 days. 3 days is not enough; the risk of resistance and relapse increases.
Vague signature: the amount, number, relation to meals and duration are not written.
In the expanded form the amount of one dose is written on the Rp. line and the number of doses with D.t.d. N. The abbreviated form: Rp.: Capsulas Omeprazoli 0.02 N. 28 / D.S. …
Diclofenac, solution in ampoules
Patient V., 38 years old
Acute lumbago (low back pain), severe pain. No gastric ulcer, kidney disease or asthma.
Prescribe 5 ampoules of diclofenac sodium 2.5% solution, 3 mL each: once a day intramuscularly.
Correct: Solutio → genitive Solutionis (take of the solution).
Nominative. After Rp. a solution is written in the genitive: Solutionis.
Accusative. A solution is written in the genitive in a prescription.
Correct: both words are in the genitive.
Nominative. The correct form: Diclofenaci natrii.
Natrio is the ablative. The genitive is natrii.
Concentration and volume
Correct: 25 mg/mL × 3 mL = 75 mg per ampoule.
25% = 250 mg/mL: one ampoule would contain 750 mg, 10 times more.
For a solution in ampoules the volume of a single ampoule is written (3 mL), and the number goes in D.t.d. N.
Correct: dispense 5 ampoules.
For drugs in ampoules the number of ampoules is shown with D.t.d. N. … in ampullis.
The dosage form is a solution in ampoules: “in ampullis” is written.
Inject 3 mL once a day deep intramuscularly, 5 days.
Correct: diclofenac solution in ampoules is injected deep intramuscularly; parenteral use is usually limited to 2–5 days.
Inject 3 mL as an intravenous bolus.
Diclofenac in ampoules is not given as an intravenous bolus; it is injected deep intramuscularly.
Inject 3 mL subcutaneously.
Subcutaneous injection is not intended: there is a risk of severe local irritation and tissue damage.
Intramuscularly.
Vague: the amount, number and duration are not written.
Percentage form: 2.5% = 2.5 g / 100 mL = 25 mg/mL. When NSAIDs are given parenterally, gastrointestinal, renal and cardiovascular risks are taken into account.
Amoxicillin, suspension for a child
Patient G., 4 years old, 16 kg
Streptococcal tonsillitis (group A beta-hemolytic streptococcus, rapid test positive). No penicillin allergy.
Prescribe amoxicillin suspension (250 mg/5 mL), 5 mL three times a day for 10 days. Calculate the total volume required.
Correct: Suspensio → Suspensionis.
This is a solution. Amoxicillin is suspended as particles that do not dissolve in water: this is a suspension.
Nominative. In a prescription the genitive is used: Suspensionis.
Correct: 5 mL × 3 times × 10 days = 150 mL.
50 mL lasts only 3 days. 5 mL × 3 × 10 days = 150 mL is needed.
Calculation error: 5 × 3 × 10 = 150 mL, not 1500.
Shake before use. Take 5 mL three times a day for 10 days.
Correct: for a suspension “shake before use” must be written. The daily dose of 750 mg ≈ 47 mg/kg is in line with the ~50 mg/kg recommended for streptococcal tonsillitis.
Take 5 mL three times a day for 10 days.
In the signature of a suspension “Shake before use” must be written: if it is not shaken the particles settle and the dose will be wrong.
Shake before use. Take 5 mL once a day for 10 days.
250 mg per day ≈ 16 mg/kg: not enough. Amoxicillin acts in a time-dependent way and has a short t½ (~1 hour): it is given 2–3 times a day.
Shake before use. Take 5 mL three times a day for 3 days.
In streptococcal tonsillitis penicillins are given for 10 days to prevent rheumatic fever.
A suspension must not be given intravenously. A child's dose is always checked per mg/kg: 16 kg × 50 mg/kg = 800 mg/day.
Eye drops for glaucoma
Patient D., 62 years old
Open-angle glaucoma, intraocular pressure 30 mm Hg. The ophthalmologist recommended a muscarinic agonist.
Prescribe 10 mL of pilocarpine hydrochloride 1% solution as eye drops.
Correct: a muscarinic agonist constricts the pupil, improves the outflow of aqueous humor and lowers the pressure.
Dangerous error! Atropine is a muscarinic antagonist: it dilates the pupil and impedes the outflow of aqueous humor. It is contraindicated in glaucoma and can trigger an acute glaucoma attack.
Nominative. In the genitive: Pilocarpini hydrochloridi.
Correct: pilocarpine eye drops come in 1–2%.
10% pilocarpine eye drops are not used: risk of a strong systemic muscarinic effect (bradycardia, bronchospasm, salivation).
1 mL does not last even a few days; eye drops are prescribed in a 5–10 mL bottle.
Eye drops. Instill 1–2 drops into both eyes three times a day.
Correct: the route, the amount and the number are shown.
Take 20 drops three times a day by mouth.
These are eye drops: not for drinking.
Instill into the eye.
Vague: how many drops and how many times a day are not written.
Eye drops are prepared sterile. To reduce systemic absorption, after instillation the inner corner of the eye is pressed for 1–2 minutes.
Eye ointment
Patient E., 25 years old
Bacterial blepharoconjunctivitis: eyelid redness, purulent discharge. No antibiotic allergy.
Prescribe 10.0 g of tetracycline 1% eye ointment.
Correct: Unguentum → Unguenti.
Nominative. In a prescription the genitive: Unguenti.
Ablative. In a prescription the genitive: Unguenti.
Substance, concentration and quantity
Tetracyclini ophthalmici 1% — 10.0
Correct: the eye ointment is 1% and sterile; the word “ophthalmici” is added.
Tetracyclini 3% — 10.0
3% tetracycline ointment is intended for the skin and is not put in the eye. For the eye a 1% ophthalmici ointment is prescribed.
An ointment is measured by mass (in grams): 10.0.
Apply behind the lower eyelid three times a day, 7 days.
Correct: the site of application, the number and the duration are exact.
Apply to the eye.
Vague: where, how many times a day and for how long are not written.
Apply a thick layer to the skin three times a day.
Eye ointment is placed behind the lower eyelid.
Eye dosage forms must be sterile. Systemic use of tetracycline is restricted in children under 8 years, while local eye ointment is used even in newborns.
Suppository for a child
Patient J., 4 years old, 17 kg
Acute respiratory infection, temperature 39.0 °C, vomiting: cannot take the drug by mouth.
Prescribe paracetamol in 0.25 g rectal suppositories (10 pieces).
Correct: after the preposition “cum” (with) the substance name is written in the ablative.
After “cum” the ablative is needed, not the genitive: Paracetamolo.
Nominative. After “cum” the ablative: Paracetamolo.
Correct: 250 mg ≈ 15 mg/kg (17 kg); the single dose for children is 10–15 mg/kg.
2.5 g = 2500 mg ≈ 147 mg/kg in one dose: a toxic dose that damages the liver.
25 mg ≈ 1.5 mg/kg: no effect.
Correct: dispense 10 such suppositories.
The number of suppositories is not shown: write D.t.d. N. 10.
M.f. pulvis — “let a powder be made”. Here the dosage form is a suppository.
Insert 1 suppository into the rectum when the temperature is above 38.5 °C; not more than 4 times a day, at least 6 hours apart.
Correct: at most 1.0 g per day ≈ 59 mg/kg, which does not exceed the permitted daily dose for children (60 mg/kg).
Take 1 suppository three times a day.
A suppository is not taken by mouth: it is inserted into the rectum.
Insert 1 suppository every 2 hours when the temperature is raised.
Every 2 hours, 12 suppositories a day = 3.0 g ≈ 176 mg/kg: toxic. The interval must be at least 6 hours.
For a suppository the dose of the active substance is written for one suppository. If the base is not stated, rectal suppositories are prepared on a 3.0 g base.
Ceftriaxone, powder in a vial
Patient Z., 50 years old, 72 kg
Community-acquired pneumonia, moderately severe. No allergy to penicillins or cephalosporins. No allergy to lidocaine.
Prescribe ceftriaxone in 1.0 g vials for 7 days: once a day intramuscularly, dissolved in 1% lidocaine.
Correct: genitive (Ceftriaxonum → Ceftriaxoni).
Nominative. The correct form: Ceftriaxoni.
Ablative. The correct form: Ceftriaxoni.
Correct: 1.0 g in one vial.
10 g: 10 times more. In adults the daily dose is usually 1–2 g, maximum 4 g.
A whole number is not written without a digit after the decimal point: 1.0.
Correct: 7 vials for 7 days.
Ceftriaxone is supplied in vials (sterile powder), not in ampoules.
The number of vials is shown with D.t.d. N.
Dissolve the powder in the vial in 3.5 mL of 1% lidocaine solution and inject deep intramuscularly once a day, 7 days.
Correct: ceftriaxone dissolved in lidocaine is given only intramuscularly.
Dissolve the powder in 1% lidocaine solution and inject intravenously once a day.
Dangerous error! Ceftriaxone diluted with lidocaine is given only intramuscularly; for intravenous use it is dissolved in water for injection.
Dissolve the powder in Ringer's solution and give by intravenous drip.
Mixing ceftriaxone with calcium-containing solutions (Ringer's) is prohibited: a calcium–ceftriaxone precipitate forms in the lungs and kidneys.

A separate prescription is written for the lidocaine solution, and the two prescriptions are separated by the # sign: # Rp.: Solutionis Lidocaini 1% — 3.5 ml / D.t.d. N. 7 in ampullis / S. To dissolve ceftriaxone.
Valerian tincture
Patient I., 40 years old
Irritability, mild difficulty falling asleep. No comorbidities, does not drink alcohol.
Prescribe 30 mL of valerian tincture: 20–25 drops three times a day.
Correct: Tinctura → Tincturae.
Nominative. In a prescription the genitive: Tincturae.
Accusative. In a prescription the genitive: Tincturae.
Name and quantity
Correct: a tincture is an officinal drug, and its concentration is not written in the prescription.
Even if valerian tincture is prepared in a 1:5 ratio, it is an officinal drug: its concentration is not written in the prescription.
300 mL is far too much for a tincture taken as 20–25 drops three times a day: usually 25–30 mL is written.
Take 20–25 drops three times a day.
Correct.
Take 20–25 mL three times a day.
mL instead of drops: this is 20 times more (1 mL ≈ 20 drops). Almost the whole bottle would be taken in one dose.
Take when sleep does not come.
Vague: the amount and number are not written.
Alcoholic tinctures are prescribed with caution to drivers and to patients who must avoid alcohol.
Dexamethasone, mass–volume form
Patient K., 33 years old
Moderate acute exacerbation of bronchial asthma. After an inhaled bronchodilator, a short course of a systemic glucocorticoid is being prescribed.
Prescribe 10 ampoules of dexamethasone solution containing 0.004 g (4 mg) per 1 mL (in mass–volume form).
Correct: genitive.
Nominative. The correct form: Dexamethasoni.
Mass and volume
Correct: mass–volume form: 0.004 g (4 mg) of substance in 1 mL of solution.
0.4 g = 400 mg in one ampoule: 100 times more.
4 g: 1000 times more.
Inject 1 mL once or twice a day, slowly intravenously or intramuscularly.
Correct: the amount, the number and the route are shown.
Inject intravenously.
Vague: the single dose and the number of times a day are not written.
Inject 10 mL as an intravenous push.
10 mL = 10 ampoules (40 mg) at once: more than prescribed, and all the ampoules run out on the very first day.
The mass–volume form equals the percent form: 0.004 g / 1 mL = 4 mg/mL = 0.4%.
Hypertension and bronchial asthma
Patient L., 58 years old
Arterial hypertension, BP 165/100 mm Hg. Comorbidity: bronchial asthma. No edema, heart rate 76/min.
Prescribe a suitable antihypertensive drug, 30 tablets.
Correct: a calcium channel blocker does not affect the bronchi and is safe in asthma.
Dangerous error! Propranolol is a nonselective beta-blocker: it also blocks β2 receptors in the bronchi and causes bronchospasm. Contraindicated in bronchial asthma.
Nominative. The correct form: Amlodipini.
Correct: 5 mg, the starting dose.
0.05 g = 50 mg: 5 times the maximum daily dose (10 mg).
5 g: a thousand times more.
Take 1 tablet once a day in the morning; taken continuously, monitor BP.
Correct: the t½ of amlodipine is 35–50 hours, so once a day is enough; hypertension is treated continuously.
Take 1 tablet 3 times a day.
Amlodipine is long-acting (t½ 35–50 hours): it is given once a day. Three times a day leads to dose accumulation and hypotension.
Take 1 tablet when you have a headache.
Arterial hypertension is treated continuously; the drug is not taken only when symptoms appear.
When choosing a drug, comorbidities are taken into account: in bronchial asthma nonselective beta-blockers are contraindicated.

Theophylline: calculate the loading dose

The patient weighs 70 kg, asthma attack, has not taken theophylline before. Vd = 0.5 L/kg, target concentration 10 mg/L, F ≈ 1. How many mg is the loading dose? (Formula: loading dose = Css × Vd / F.)

Vd = 0.5 × 70 = 35 L. Loading dose = 10 mg/L × 35 L / 1 = 350 mg (≈ 5 mg/kg). The loading dose ensures that Css is reached immediately; the subsequent maintenance dose depends on clearance. If the patient has taken theophylline before, the loading dose is reduced or not given.
